Constitutional Amendment
Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers
Amends the California Constitution to remove the choice of a successor from recall elections. Allows vacancies created by recalls to be filled under succession rules for state officers.
SPUR's Recommendation
Prop. 5 would help California avoid scenarios in which a successor can take statewide office with only a small plurality of votes. It would eliminate an incentive structure that has made recalls an attractive strategic partisan tool for removing elected officials without majority support. Replacing a plurality-rule special election with an institutional process tied to officials who themselves were elected by a majority of voters represents a more democratic and coherent outcome than the status quo.
Vote YES
What Prop. 5 Would Do
Proposition 5 would amend the California Constitution to change how state officer recall elections work in three key ways. 1
First, when voters choose to recall an elected official, they also choose that person’s successor on the same ballot. Prop. 5 would eliminate the successor election and instead fill the office through existing constitutional succession rules. These rules require the governor to fill non-legislative office vacancies (e.g., secretary of state, attorney general, controller) by appointment, and special elections to fill legislative office vacancies (senator, assemblymember).
Second, if a governor is recalled, Prop. 5 would require the lieutenant governor to assume the governorship for the remainder of the term. If the governor is successfully recalled before the close of nomination for the next statewide election, a special election would be held at the next statewide primary. This special election would prevent an unelected appointed governor from holding office for a full four-year term. 2
Third, Prop. 5 removes the prohibition on recalled officers running for the same office in a subsequent special election to fill their seat.
State Senator Josh Newman, who was recalled in 2019, and Assemblymember Isaac Bryan introduced the measure in 2023. The legislation was referred to the 2026 state ballot and requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass.
The Backstory
California voters authorized the recall process in 1911 through a ballot measure that passed with 76.8% of the vote. 3 The current recall process for state officers requires that voters elect a successor on the same ballot. The recalled official is prohibited from appearing as a candidate on the successor ballot. If a recall is successful, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes takes office immediately. 4
Current voting requirements for candidates to win regular elections (with two final candidates) differ from those for candidates in recall elections (with multiple candidates). A candidate can prevail in a recall successor race with a plurality of votes (the most votes, even if it's not more than 50%) rather than a majority (more than 50%). All voters may vote for a replacement candidate on the same ballot as the recall, regardless of whether they voted yes or no on the initial recall question. In the successful 2003 gubernatorial recall, Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger replaced Governor Gray Davis with only 48.6% of the vote. The attempted 2021 recall of Governor Gavin Newsom renewed attention to the process.
Most states that allow recalls already use either established succession rules or a separate special election. Since 1913, 179 recall attempts have targeted California state elected officials; 11 qualified for the ballot, and six officials were ultimately recalled. 5
The current recall system benefits the minority party in state politics because it offers an additional opportunity outside the normal election cycle to elect minority-party candidates. This election would occur at a moment of discontent with the majority-party officeholder, which is likely to increase the minority party’s chances of electing its candidate. In the near term, this advantage would favor Republicans, given that Democrats have held a majority in both the state legislature and the governorship since 2011.
State Gubernatorial Recall Provisions
Source: Ballotpedia, States with gubernatorial recall provisions (https://ballotpedia.org/States_with_gubernatorial_recall_provisions) .
Equity Impacts
Prop. 5’s equity implications are largely procedural rather than direct, but two dynamics are worth weighing.
First, the current successor-election system allows a candidate to take statewide office with a plurality of the vote — sometimes well under 50% — which can dilute the influence of any single bloc of voters, including communities of color. The current dynamic of off-cycle election timing is known to widen underrepresentation by shrinking and skewing the electorate toward already-engaged, disproportionately white and older voters. 6 Prop. 5 would increase the likelihood that gubernatorial successor elections are pushed to an on-cycle election, reducing the risk of underrepresentation from various voting blocs.
Second, eliminating the simultaneous successor vote does reduce one direct opportunity for voters to weigh in on a successor, which could be read as narrowing immediate civic participation. However, the constitutional succession process (e.g., replacing a recalled governor with the lieutenant governor, who was elected statewide) preserves a democratically legitimate alternative.
Pros
Prop. 5 would reduce the risk that a recall election would install an officeholder who lacks majority support. The change would align recall outcomes more closely with how California fills other vacancies.
The measure would discourage political actors from using recalls as a strategic end-run around the normal election cycle by calculating they could win a low-turnout plurality race even without majority public support.
It would provide more predictability and stability in succession for gubernatorial recalls because the lieutenant governor (already elected statewide) fills the vacancy under established, non-ad-hoc rules rather than through a compressed, high-stakes special election.
It would clarify decisions for voters who may be confused by the current successor election process, which is inherently more complicated than a single choice to recall or not recall an officer.
It would reduce the likelihood that voters would choose not to recall an elected officer because they are concerned about their successor. It would increase the likelihood that votes are cast to address actual non-partisan concerns about the officer targeted by the recall election.
Cons
Prop. 5 would require an additional election for recalls in the legislature, which could increase the cost of filling a vacancy in those seats.
The measure would allow appointees who were not elected to hold the governorship and preside over a lame-duck period, thereby potentially weakening the leadership’s ability to enact strong policy.
Vote YES

Proposition 5 would amend the California Constitution to change how state officer recall elections work in three key ways.^1^
First, when voters choose to recall an elected official, they also choose that person’s successor on the same ballot.
Prop.
5 would eliminate the successor election and instead fill the office through existing constitutional succession rules.
These rules require the governor to fill non-legislative office vacancies (e.g., secretary of state, attorney general, controller) by appointment, and special elections to fill legislative office vacancies (senator, assemblymember).
Second, if a governor is recalled, Prop.
5 would require the lieutenant governor to assume the governorship for the remainder of the term.
If the governor is successfully recalled before the close of nomination for the next statewide election, a special election would be held at the next statewide primary.
This special election would prevent an unelected appointed governor from holding office for a full four-year term.^2^
Third, Prop.
5 removes the prohibition on recalled officers running for the same office in a subsequent special election to fill their seat.

Proposition 5
Delay replacing recalled state officials
Under current law, after choosing whether to recall an elected official, voters are asked who should replace them. This constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by state lawmakers, would delay the election of a successor until a separate election. The recalled officer would be allowed to run in that election. If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over their duties until a new governor is elected. The California Legislature put this measure on the ballot.
Weigh the arguments.
Take our quizzes to learn more about each proposition.
BEGIN → (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/propositions/quizzes)
Support
Oppose
Summary
Support
Proposition 5 is a constitutional amendment born out of a proposal from the secretary of state’s office following the unsuccessful recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. Secretary of State Shirley Weber told lawmakers her office felt a recall election should focus on whether the elected official should be recalled, not whether other potential candidates would be better in the role. Democrat Josh Newman, who was successfully recalled from his state Senate seat in 2018, authored the measure, saying it would reduce the “political gamesmanship” that elevates candidates who otherwise wouldn’t receive a majority of votes.
Oppose
Opponents including the California Republican Party and Election Integrity Project, which advocates for voter ID requirements and restrictions on mail-in voting, argue that allowing the lieutenant governor to assume the governor’s position if the governor were recalled would dissuade people from participating in a recall election. Almost all legislative Republicans also opposed it, arguing that it would dilute the power of voters while protecting incumbents. The current recall process is how former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, was first elected in 2003.

PROPOSITION 5
This amendment proposed by Senate Constitutional
Amendment 1 of the 2023–2024 Regular Session
(Resolution Chapter 204, Statutes of 2024) expressly
amends the California Constitution by amending
sections thereof; therefore, existing provisions
proposed to be deleted are printed in strikeout type
and new provisions proposed to be added are printed in
italic type to indicate that they are new.
PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO
ARTICLES II AND V
First—That Section 15 of Article II thereof is amended
to read:
SEC. 15. (a) An election to determine whether to
recall an officer and, if appropriate, to elect a successor
shall be called by the Governor and held not less than
60 days nor more than 80 days from the date of
certification of sufficient signatures.
(b) A recall election may be conducted within 180 days
from the date of certification of sufficient signatures in
order that the election may be consolidated with the
next regularly scheduled election occurring wholly or
partially within the same jurisdiction in which the recall
election is held, if the number of voters eligible to vote
at that next regularly scheduled election equal at least
50 percent of all the voters eligible to vote at the recall
election.
(c) If the majority vote on the question is to recall, the
officer is removed and, if there is a candidate, the
candidate who receives a plurality is the successor. The
officer may not be a candidate, nor shall there be any
candidacy for an office filled pursuant to subdivision (d)
of Section 16 of Article VI. and the office shall be
vacant. The vacancy shall be filled in accordance with
this Constitution and statute, provided that the officer
who was the subject of the recall election shall not be
appointed to fill the vacancy in that office.

Second—That Section 17 of Article II thereof is
amended to read:
SEC. 17. If recall of the Governor or Secretary of
State is initiated, the recall duties of that office shall be
performed by the Lieutenant Governor Secretary of
State or Controller, respectively. If recalls of the
Governor and Secretary of State are initiated at the
same time, the recall duties of both offices shall be
performed by the Controller.
Third—That Section 10 of Article V thereof is amended
to read:
SEC. 10. (a) The Lieutenant Governor shall become
Governor when a vacancy occurs in the office of
Governor.
(b) Notwithstanding subdivision (c) of Section 15 of
Article II, if the Governor is removed from office by
recall, the Lieutenant Governor shall become Governor
for the remainder of the unexpired term. If the Governor
is removed from office by recall before the close of the
nomination period for the next statewide election during
the first two years of the Governor’s term, a special
election shall be called to replace the Governor and
shall be consolidated with the statewide primary
election and, if necessary, the subsequent statewide
general election. If a candidate receives a majority of
the votes in the special election that is consolidated
with the statewide primary election, that candidate
shall become Governor for the remainder of the
unexpired term. If no candidate receives a majority of
the votes, the top two vote-getters shall compete in a
special election consolidated with the subsequent
statewide general election, and the winner of that
election shall become Governor for the remainder of the
unexpired term.
(c) The Lieutenant Governor shall act as Governor
during the impeachment, absence from the State, or
other temporary disability of the Governor or of a
Governor-elect who fails to take office.
(d) The Legislature shall provide an order of
precedence after the Lieutenant Governor for
succession to the office of Governor and for the
temporary exercise of the Governor’s functions.
(e) The Supreme Court has exclusive jurisdiction to
determine all questions arising under this section.
(f) Standing to raise questions of vacancy or temporary
disability is vested exclusively in a body provided by
statute.

Proposition 5: Statewide Officers
Proposition 5: Statewide Officers
Proposition 5: Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Recall Reform, Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment
Summary
The California Senate introduced Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (SCA) in January of 2023. As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters. The Senate passed the bill in February of 2024 and the Assembly passed an amended version in August of 2024. The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process. Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled. If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law. Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor. If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
The financial impact would depend on how often recalls occur and which offices are involved. Costs could increase by millions of dollars when a recall creates a vacancy that requires a separate special election, particularly for legislative offices. At the same time, eliminating replacement candidates from recall ballots could save millions in some elections by reducing ballot and election-material costs. Overall, Proposition 5 could result in either costs or savings of potentially millions of dollars per recall election, although the effect would be very small compared with the state’s overall budget.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports changing California’s recall process so voters would decide only whether to remove an official, with the vacancy filled later under state law. A recalled official could run again, and the Lieutenant Governor would generally replace a recalled Governor.
NO: A “no” vote supports keeping the current recall process, in which voters decide whether to remove an official and simultaneously vote on who should replace that official if the recall succeeds.

Opponents argue that voters should have the right to choose a Governor’s replacement at the time when they approve a recall.   - So the recalled officer cannot be appointed, but can run in a special election. That's the "bizarre flaw" the Chronicle noted.

2. Removes a perverse incentive: a faction can use recall as an end-run around regular elections in an off-cycle, low-turnout election, installing a candidate with minimal support. PROP 5: Recall Reform (Eliminate the Replacement Question)
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-09/California%20Decides_Proposition%205.pdf)
Research
Quick Facts
Key Questions
Risks & Benefits
California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.”
Type: Legislatively referred constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by the legislature rather than by citizen signatures.
A vote YES means: A recall becomes a single yes-or-no vote on removing the official. There is no second replacement question. If the official is removed, the seat is filled the same way any midterm vacancy is filled, and the recalled official is allowed to run in any special election (with the exception of the governor, who would be immediately succeeded by the lieutenant governor).
A vote NO means: California keeps the current two-question recall. Voters answer whether to remove the official and, on the same ballot, choose a replacement from a separate list. The targeted official cannot be on that replacement list.
Sponsor/proponent: Former state senator Josh Newman (D), the measure’s author. Coauthored in the Assembly by Isaac Bryan (D). Backed by groups including the League of Women Voters of California and California Common Cause.
On the ballot because: The legislature passed SCA 1 largely along party lines (Senate 31–7 on February 1, 2024; Assembly 59–17 on August 30, 2024; and Senate concurrence 32–8 on August 31, 2024). A constitutional amendment referred by the legislature does not need the governor’s signature and goes directly to voters.
Full legal text: SCA 1, Resolution Chapter 204 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)
LAO analysis: Legislative Analyst’s Office, ballot analysis (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 5 rewrites how California—one of nineteen states that permits recall elections for state officials (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials)—recalls a state officer. Dating back to 1913, eleven recall efforts have qualified for the ballot (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present). Only six California state officeholders have been recalled: five members of the legislature and one governor. Today a recall ballot asks two questions at once: first, should the official be removed; second, if removed, who should replace them. The replacement is chosen by plurality from a separate list of candidates, and the official facing recall is barred from appearing on that list.
Prop 5 removes the second question. A recall would become a single up-or-down vote on removal. If a majority votes to remove, the seat becomes vacant and is filled the same way any other midterm vacancy in that office is filled under existing law.
If the governor is recalled before the close of the nomination period for the next statewide election during the first two years of the term, the lieutenant governor would serve until voters elect a new governor at a future statewide election. If the recall occurs later, the lieutenant governor would serve the remainder of the term. For most other statewide offices, under the rules that already govern vacancies, a vacancy is filled by gubernatorial appointment and for legislative seats it is filled by special election.
The measure also repeals the current bar on the recalled official running to keep the seat. Under Prop 5, that official may not be appointed to the vacancy but is free to run in any special election held to fill it. The amendment adds administrative plumbing as well. It assigns the secretary of state the recall duties normally handled by the governor when the governor is the target, and it shifts those duties to the controller if the governor and secretary of state are both facing recall at the same time.
2. The legal language
Full text: SCA 1, “Elections: Recall of State Officers,” Resolution Chapter 204 (2024), California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)
Key language:
“If the majority vote on the question is to recall, the officer is removed and the office shall be vacant. The vacancy shall be filled in accordance with this Constitution and statute, provided that the officer who was the subject of the recall election shall not be appointed to fill the vacancy in that office.”
What it amends: SCA 1 amends sections 15 and 17 of Article II of the California Constitution, the article that governs recalls, and Section 10 of Article V, which covers gubernatorial succession. Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot repeal it on its own once voters approve it.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Authored by former state senator Josh Newman, with Assemblymember Isaac Bryan as a coauthor. Support comes from good government groups such as the League of Women Voters of California and California Common Cause. Opposition includes the Election Integrity Project California and the California Taxpayers Association. The legislative votes ran along party lines, with Democrats in favor and Republicans opposed.
What? A single removal question on the recall ballot, no replacement question, the seat filled by the ordinary vacancy rules, and the recalled official permitted to run in any special election.
Where? Statewide, written into the California Constitution, applying to recalls of state officers including the governor, other statewide officers, and legislators.
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. It takes effect the day after the election if approved.
Why? Proponents say the two-question format created a structural flaw, exposed in 2003, where an official can be removed by a majority and replaced by a candidate who wins only a small plurality of a crowded field. Their stated goal is to prevent a replacement who commands far less support than the official being ousted.
4. Trade-offs
In 2003, voters recalled Gov. Gray Davis, with about 55.4 percent voting to remove him. On the same ballot, Arnold Schwarzenegger won the replacement race with roughly 48.6 percent in a field of 135 candidates. Davis was removed by a clear majority, and his successor took office with a plurality. The 2021 recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom put the risk in sharper relief. Newsom was retained by about 61.9 percent to 38.1 percent, so the replacement question never mattered. But had the vote to remove been a bare majority, the leading replacement candidate could have become governor with a fraction of the statewide vote, far below the share that voted to keep Newsom. That mismatch is the core case for Prop 5: A single question cannot install a minority winner.
The other side is that the two-question ballot lets voters remove an official and choose a replacement on the same day. Prop 5 separates those steps. Under the measure, recalling a governor hands the office to the lieutenant governor, who may be of the same party and the same politics the recall was meant to reject. For other offices, the seat can be filled by appointment, which moves the choice from voters to officeholders, at least until a special election. Critics argue this weakens the recall as a direct check, because voters lose the guarantee that removal produces a chosen replacement, and it can hand the reformers’ win to a successor they did not pick.
The current system guarantees voters a replacement choice but can produce a minority winner. Prop 5 forecloses the minority winner but can produce a successor who voters did not select and, in the case of an appointed statewide officer, did not vote on at all. Which risk matters more depends on what a voter thinks a recall is for: punishing an official or choosing a new one.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
Prop 5 closes the minority-winner loophole. A recall could no longer replace a majority-removed official with a plurality candidate from a crowded field, the outcome the 2003 recall produced.
It simplifies the ballot to a single, clear question about removal, which reduces voter confusion and the strategic gamesmanship of a large replacement field.
It removes the incentive, cited by the author, for a candidate to trigger a recall mainly as a low-threshold path to an office they could not win in a regular election.
It treats a recall vacancy like any other vacancy, giving the process consistent and predictable succession rules already in the state constitution and statute.
It ends the current bar on the targeted official, letting that person make their case to voters in any special election rather than being excluded by rule.
It could lower ballot and election administration costs, potentially by millions of dollars in some recall elections, by removing the replacement candidate question.
Potential risks
Removing a governor hands the office to the lieutenant governor, who may share the recalled governor’s party and politics, so voters could remove an official and get more of the same.
For statewide offices filled by appointment, the replacement choice shifts from voters to the governor, at least until any special election, which weakens the recall as a direct citizen check.
Separating removal from replacement can leave a seat vacant or in caretaker hands for a period, creating uncertainty about who holds the office and for how long.
The change is a permanent constitutional amendment shaped by two high-profile gubernatorial recalls, yet it governs recalls of every state officer, including legislators, where the dynamics differ.
If a separate special election is needed to fill the resulting vacancy, state and local election administration costs could increase by millions of dollars.
6. Open questions
When a governor is recalled, how long would the lieutenant governor serve, and under what timing rules would a special election be held to let voters choose a successor?
For statewide offices filled by appointment, how long could an appointed successor hold the seat before voters get a say?
Does letting the recalled official run in a later special election blunt the reform, or is it a fair chance to seek vindication at the ballot box?
Would a single-question recall make recalls easier to launch, since organizers no longer need a marquee replacement candidate to rally behind?
Does the measure change the incentives to attempt a recall at all, and in which direction?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
A recall does two things: remove an official and decide who comes next. Prop 5 keeps the first and changes the second. Before you vote, ask whether a recall should guarantee you a say in the replacement or whether it should be a clean up-or-down vote on removal alone.
The 2003 recall showed a majority can oust a governor while a plurality picks the successor. Prop 5 fixes that, but it can hand a recalled governor’s seat to a lieutenant governor of the same party. Which outcome bothers you more: A minority winner or a successor you did not choose?

Endorsement: Prop 5 has a flaw so bizarre even its author doesn’t like it
Proposition 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 8, 2026
So much has happened in American politics since 2021 that the recall election of California Gov. Gavin Newsom, which he overwhelmingly defeated, feels like a distant memory.
Proposition 5 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot puts recalls back in the spotlight.
Endorsement guide: S.F. Chronicle Endorsements for the 2026 California Election (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/california-sf-election-endorsements/)
Also: Y (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/supreme-court-judge-california-22431608.php)es or no? Here are the Chronicle’s endorsements for California Supreme Court and appeals courts (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/supreme-court-judge-california-22431608.php)
Authored by (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1) former Democratic state Sen. Josh Newman of Fullerton — who was recalled in 2018, won reelection in 2020 and lost again in 2024 — Prop 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Here’s how the current process works:
To recall a statewide official, proponents must gather signatures totaling at least 12% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the prior election. For the Newsom recall, that threshold was 1.3 million signatures (https://admin.cdn.sos.ca.gov/elections/ccrov/2025/march/25024ra.pdf). To recall members of the state Assembly and Senate, the minimum number of signatures is 20% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the last election — for Newman’s recall, that threshold was about 63,600 signatures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2018-news-releases-and-advisories/recall-signatures-senate-district-29-certified).
Once a recall qualifies, voters then receive a ballot with two questions — one, should this official be recalled, and two, who should replace them? — and a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority votes in favor of the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
The two-question setup is confusing — only six other states use it (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials). And permitting someone to be elected without majority support is undemocratic. Furthermore, given the distraction and price of recalls — Newsom’s cost about $200 million during (https://apnews.com/article/elections-california-legislature-gavin-newsom-state-legislature-f8b78745cc5376dc4836d914352f2116) the most fraught moments of the pandemic — they should be reserved for cases of serious misconduct or abject unfitness, not petty grievances.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Even though only 11 recalls of state-level officials have qualified for the ballot since 1913, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), California could benefit from raising the bar. Its signature-gathering threshold is among the lowest in the nation (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/Report266.pdf).
But Prop 5 doesn’t grapple with this issue.
Instead, it would eliminate the second question from the recall ballot, meaning voters would decide only whether the official should be removed.
If a majority says yes, one of three things would happen:
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would automatically step into the role. If the recall happens in the first half of a governor’s four-year term before the nomination period ends for the next statewide election, the lieutenant governor would serve until that election takes place and voters choose the next governor. But if the recall happens after that point, the lieutenant governor would finish the rest of the governor’s term.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
If another statewide official — such as the lieutenant governor, attorney general or secretary of state — is recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement. The governor already follows this process for statewide officials who die, resign or accept a different job.
And if a member of the state Legislature is recalled, the governor would call a special election for their replacement — mirroring the existing process for a lawmaker who dies, resigns or takes a different job. Proposition 5 could change California’s recall elections. Here is our endorsement | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 5, 2026 8:16 AM
Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html) seeks to fundamentally change how California conducts recall elections for members of the Legislature and constitutional officers elected statewide. Such elections have been rare in California.
According to theLegislative Analyst’s Office, (https://lao.ca.gov/) only 11 state recall efforts targeting nine legislators and two governors have qualified for the ballot since 1913. In 2003, Gray Davis (https://www.modbee.com/opinion/opn-columns-blogs/article251385288.html) became the only California governor to be recalled, a fate that also befell five state legislators over the years. The last statewide recall effort to qualify for the ballot was the unsuccessful campaign to oust Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/editorials/article253266413.html)
Under current law, voters are asked two questions in the same election when a recall effort qualifies for the ballot. The first is whether a state officer should be recalled. The second is who should replace that officer from a field of hopefuls seeking consideration if a recall is successful. In 2003, 135 candidates wanted to succeed Davis. In 2021, there were 46 candidates vying for Newsom’s job.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html)
If Prop. 5 is approved by state voters in November, the second question will be eliminated.
In future statewide recalls that gather enough signatures to qualify for the ballot, Californians would only vote yes or no on whether an officer should be recalled. If a state recall of a member of the Legislature was successful, that office would remain vacant until a special election was held. If a constitutional officer were recalled, the vacancies would be filled by the governor. Should a future governor be recalled in the first two years of office, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until a special election was held. If a governor were recalled later in the term, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until the next scheduled election.
This would be a longer process, but also one that’s more thoughtful, deliberate and — most importantly — respects the democratic norm of majority rule.
It’s why our combined editorial boards representing The Sacramento Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, Fresno Bee and San Luis Obispo Tribune endorse Prop. 5.
Recall elections in California
Since California voters approved the recall process in 1911, five replacement candidates have been elected after six officials were removed from office with less than 50% of the vote. In California recall elections, the candidate who receives the most votes wins, unlike in a special election, where a candidate must win a majority.
This creates a conundrum of a recalled official garnering more voter support than the replacement candidate who “wins” the recall.
In the 2018 recall of former stateSen. Josh Newman, for instance, (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article145349124.html) his replacement, Republican Ling Ling Chang, came out on top with just under 34% of the vote. Newman points out that he had more votes in his favor; nearly 42% of voters opposed his recall.
“So I got more votes by way of ‘no, don’t kick him out,’ than she got by ‘yes, please put her in,’” Newman said.
Newman won back his Senate seat in the next regular election and then went on to write Prop. 5 (https://www.kcra.com/article/california-voters-prop-5-changes-recall-election-process/73175034).
One of the proposition’s most outspoken opponents is Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a former talk radio host who pushed for Newman’s recall in 2017.
How Prop. 5 opponents feel
DeMaio sees Prop. 5 as an attempt by the ruling party to evade recalls. “What they want to do is create a situation where politicians trying to fend off a recall can say, ‘Don’t vote for the recall or else you won’t be represented for 12 months. You’ll lose your voice,’” he told us.
Actually, Article II, Section 15 of the California Constitution, says a recall election must be held within 60 and 80 days of recall petition signatures being certified. The election may be held within 180 days of certification if it is consolidated with the next regularly scheduled election.
Arguments against Prop. 5 ignore that the current system created instances where replacement candidates got elected with less than 50% of the vote.
They decry the cost of conducting special elections and oppose that Prop. 5 would allow a recalled official to run in a special election to fill the vacancy.
There have been 182 attempts (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present) to recall state officials in California. Eleven of those made the ballot, and only six were successful.
Some view the current recall system as “a weapon for political operators (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5.pdf) to undo election results they don’t like,” to quote the League of Women Voters and others.
Prop. 5 cannot put an end to the political gamesmanship, but it can safeguard the will of the voters by following the principle of majority rule.
McClatchy Media’s California editorial board strongly urges a “yes” vote on Proposition 5.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> Is a hissy fit worth $200 million (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2022-02-03/california-recall-election-cost-200-million-dollars)?
That was the tab in 2021, when California held a recall election (https://www.latimes.com/topic/newsom-recall) less than a year before Gov. Gavin Newsom was set to face voters.
There was angst —the COVID-19 pandemic was raging (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-08-19/l-a-county-covid-19-deaths-top-25000-as-delta-spreads). There was anger — the lifesaving restrictions (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-12-13/california-orders-statewide-mask-order-starting-wednesday) imposed by Washington and Sacramento made daily living a chore (https://www.latimes.com/science/coronavirus-one-year-later) and drove many small businesses to the brink. Others went clear over the edge (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2020-10-29/coronavirus-pandemic-small-business-southern-california).
There was also no small amount of political opportunism at play.
The recall gave Newsom’s critics, mainly on the right, a chance to try to chase the Democrat from an office (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-08-27/recall-backers-have-california-ideas-beyond-newsom-defeat) that Republicans, under normal circumstances, stood little chance of winning.
Advertisement
In the end, the recall effort amounted to scarcely more than a partisan tantrum. The result — 61.9% voting no, 38.1% voting yes (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-09-14/recall-election-california-newsom-results) — matched the outcome of the 2018 gubernatorial race (https://www.latimes.com/politics/la-pol-ca-california-governor-race-20181106-story.html) down to the decimal. All that money and effort wasted on an election in which voters said pretty much, yep, we meant what we said. Not too long after, they gave Newsom a second term (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2022-11-08/2022-california-election-governor-newsom-dahle-results).
The plebiscite, and its pointlessness (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-09-15/newsom-california-recall-election-costly-lessons), underscored the many flaws inherent in California’s recall system. In November, voters will get a chance to remedy at least one of them, eliminating the chance a candidate could take office with just marginal support from voters.

One choice, not two
Currently, a recall election is conducted in two parts. Voters are asked whether a lawmaker should be removed and, if so, who their replacement should be. If the incumbent is ousted, whoever gets the most votes takes their place, even if they fall well shy of attaining majority support. (Which is not out of the question in a large multi-candidate field; in 2003, 135 people were on the ballot (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-27-me-recallqa27-story.html), vying to replace Gov. Gray Davis (https://www.latimes.com/la-100703recall_lat-story.html).)
Among its provisions, Proposition 5 would amend the state Constitution so that voters would be asked a simple yes-or-no question: Do you wish to recall the incumbent? If so, the lieutenant governor would serve as governor for the rest of the ousted executive’s term — unless the recall occurred during the first two years a governor was in office and before the filing deadline for the next statewide election.
In that case, a special election would be held on the same date as the next primary and a candidate receiving a majority of votes would serve out the governor’s term. If no candidate received a majority, the top-two finishers would face each other in a November runoff, with the winner taking over as governor.
Still there?
Proposition 5 has two benefits. It would save taxpayer dollars by consolidating elections and it would enhance the legitimacy and political standing of a replacement governor by ensuring he or she assumed office with at least 50% support.
But there’s still more to be done (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2022-06-23/california-recall-reform-efforts-stall).
Ending political promiscuity
California makes it way too easy to qualify a gubernatorial recall measure.
Of the 19 states that allow their governor to be booted, California is by far the most permissive. Forcing an election requires signatures reflecting just 12% of the ballots cast in the prior gubernatorial contest. In Newsom’s case, proponents needed just under 1.5 million signatures in a state with more than 22 million voters and nearly 40 million residents.
Not exactly a thundering roar.
The threshold should be higher and the reasons for kicking a governor out of office should be more serious, such as corruption, official malfeasance or conviction for a serious crime. Not just because a governor is a member of the opposite party (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2024-03-01/newsom-recall-sore-losers-are-undermining-democracy), orpeople on the losing end (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-04-13/newsom-recall-revolt-red-vs-blue-california) of an election are unhappy with the result.

When California Governor Gray Davis was the subject of a recall effort in 2003, he said in a televised speech (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-20-me-davis20-story.htmlhttps:/www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-20-me-davis20-story.html) at UCLA that he thought the recall would damage “the very fabric of our democracy.”
Elected officials may not like to see accountability arrive earlier than expected, but that doesn’t make Californians’ recall powers a threat to democracy.
While Proposition 5 doesn’t attack the people’s ability to hold a recall election, it does tinker with how a replacement candidate is selected.

Endorsement: Voters should support the Measure M bond to fix Gilroy schools (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-voters-should-support-the-measure-m-bond-to-fix-gilroy-schools/)
We urge voters to reject it.
Proposition 5 would eliminate the election of a replacement candidate on the same ballot as a recall. Currently a recall ballot has two questions: 1) Should the elected official be removed, and 2) Choose a candidate to replace that official if the recall is successful.
The measure would remove question 2, eliminating the simultaneous election for a replacement. Instead, if a state official other than a governor was recalled, the office would become vacant and would be filled by special election or appointment, according to existing law. If a governor was recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over and serve until the end of the term or until a special election could be held, depending on timing.
Under current law, a recalled official is barred from running as a replacement candidate in the special election to fill the seat. Proposition 5 changes that as well. In a special election to replace a recalled official, the recalled official could be on the ballot.
These changes turn a process to remove officials from power into a cynical blueprint to keep power in the hands of the same officials. It makes a mockery of the recall, which was designed to empower voters to remove and immediately replace an officeholder for any reason, whether the officeholder thinks the reason is sufficient or not.
Rejecting Proposition 5 is also about preserving the state’s ability to empower unique and independent political voices.
Under current rules, officials who are recalled are succeeded by the candidate seeking that official’s job who gets the most votes at the same time as the recall. This process is why Arnold Schwarzenegger was able to quickly replace the deeply unpopular Davis.
Nearly one million more Californians voted to recall Davis than to retain him, and the Republican Schwarzenegger won a plurality of the replacement vote after running as a pro-business social liberal who wanted the state to lead the global response (https://www.kqed.org/science/1931206/californias-a-team-on-climate-moonbeam-and-the-governator) to climate change.
But if Proposition 5 had been in place, Davis would have been succeeded by Lt. Gov. Cruz Bustamante. He was an uninspiring but mostly baggage-free politician who would have likely been the favorite in a subsequent regular or special election in California to finish Davis’ term, even against Schwarzenegger.
Changing the California Constitution in a way that creates even bigger obstacles to electing independent-minded candidates — while stripping the people of their primary tool of accountability — is a bad idea.
Reject Proposition 5.

Now, I have a thorough picture. Let me weigh and decide.

Consideration framework: Which vote better serves California's democratic governance, taking into account (a) legitimacy of officeholders, (b) voter empowerment/accountability, (c) practical costs and stability, (d) partisan fairness/entrenchment, (e) drafting quality.

Pro (YES) substantive merits:
1. Majority-rule legitimacy: Every one of California's six successful state recalls installed a successor with less than 50% of the vote; in Newman's 2018 recall, the successor (Ling Ling Chang) got ~34% while ~42% voted against the recall — the successor had fewer votes than those wanting the incumbent kept. That's a genuine democratic inversion. In 2021, a bare-majority recall could have installed a governor with ~28% support. Prop 5 guarantees that a gubernatorial successor either was elected statewide by a majority (Lt Gov) or wins a majority in a top-two special election.
2. Consistency: aligns recall vacancies with existing vacancy rules (death/resignation), reducing ad hoc complexity; most recall states don't use the same-day successor question (only ~6 others do).
3. Removes conflict of interest: currently the Lt Gov — the direct beneficiary of a successful gubernatorial recall — administers the recall process; Prop 5 shifts that to the SOS (and Controller if SOS also recalled). That's an unambiguous improvement.
4. Deters recalls used as a partisan shortcut/prize lottery and reduces the incentive to force $200M+ off-cycle elections with 46–135-candidate ballots. Recalls remain fully intact as a removal tool (signature thresholds unchanged, majority removal unchanged).
5. Nonpartisan good-government backing: League of Women Voters of California, California Common Cause, former FPPC Chair Dan Schnur (a Republican), Secretary of State Weber, McClatchy CA editorial board, LA Times columnists Barabak & Skelton, SPUR. LAO finds negligible fiscal effect (<0.1% of General Fund).

Con (NO) substantive merits:
1. Voters lose the simultaneous replacement choice; for statewide offices other than governor, the Governor (with legislative confirmation) appoints a successor who could serve the rest of the term — no election at all. That converts a voter-initiated removal into an executive patronage appointment, and in a one-party state effectively guarantees the successor shares the removed official's politics.
2. Legislative recalls leave districts unrepresented for months while a special election is called and held (potentially 4-6+ months, longer if consolidated) — and cost millions.
3. Drafting flaw: it deletes the constitutional bar on the recalled officer running to reclaim the very seat they were removed from (even the author says he doesn't know why it's there). That materially weakens removal and could let an ousted official — with an intact war chest — immediately run back.
4. It doesn't address the more fundamental problems (very low signature threshold — 12% statewide; no requirement of cause), so it's a partial reform that takes away a voter right while leaving the "easy to trigger" problem.
5. Partisan entrenchment: passed along party lines by the majority party after a failed recall of their governor; authored by a man who was himself recalled. Hoover/Mercury News argue it removes the minority party's realistic path to statewide power and advantages "independent-minded" outsiders (Schwarzenegger). Under Prop 5, Davis would have been succeeded by Lt Gov Bustamante — the same party voters were rejecting.
6. Public opinion strongly opposes (35-59 in September; 45-52 in October), suggesting voters' gut reaction is to preserve their right to choose a replacement.

Which way? This is genuinely contested, but the question asks for a decision. Let me think about what a careful, impartial analyst would conclude.

Key trade-off: Is the plurality-successor problem serious enough to justify shifting successor selection away from voters (to appointments/succession)?

I think the plurality-successor problem is real but it is a symptom; the deeper problem is the low threshold to trigger a recall and the absence of any cause requirement. Prop 5 does not fix the trigger; it only changes the outcome. In fact, by removing the "prize," it could reduce recall attempts — a plausible deterrent effect. That's a benefit.

But the concern about gubernatorial succession: under Prop 5, if a governor is recalled in the second half of the term, the Lt Gov serves the remainder with no election. Under current law, voters would choose a replacement. That is a genuine reduction of voter choice for the single most important office. But note: the Lt Gov was elected statewide by majority (top-two runoff) in the same election as the governor — arguably as legitimate as a plurality winner in a 46-candidate recall field. And this mirrors what happens on death/resignation (e.g., if Newsom had resigned to become ambassador, Eleni Kounalakis would have become governor for the remainder). So Prop 5's gubernatorial rule isn't novel; it extends existing succession and adds an election in early-term recalls.

For the other statewide offices: appointment by Governor (with legislative confirmation) mirrors existing vacancy law too.

So actually, Prop 5 is best understood as: "treat recall like any other vacancy" — consistent, predictable, and requiring majority-elected successors. The one deviation is for early-term gubernatorial recalls, where it adds a majority-based special election (an improvement over existing vacancy law).

The self-run provision is a wart but arguably not disqualifying: the recalled officer must still win a majority in a special election (for legislators/governor), and cannot be appointed. In practice, someone just recalled by majority vote is unlikely to win a special election months later — and if they did, that's voters changing their minds (like Newman himself, who won his seat back in 2020).

Hmm, but here's the thing: allowing the recalled official to run in the special election could make recalls effectively "do-overs" of the regular election. For legislators, the recalled incumbent could win back the seat — meaning the recall accomplished nothing except cost. That's a real defect. But it also cuts the other way: it makes the recall itself less attractive as a cheap path to office for challengers, because the incumbent can just run back and win in a head-to-head majority election.

Balance: On the central question — which system produces more legitimate, accountable government — I think Prop 5's approach is defensible and mildly better: it eliminates minority-plurality installation, resolves an obvious conflict of interest, and standardizes succession. The costs (delayed representation for legislative seats, gubernatorial appointment of some successors, the odd self-run provision) are real but modest, and largely mirror existing vacancy rules that Californians already accept.

But wait — let me consider a counterweight more seriously: does Prop 5 entrench the majority party and reduce electoral competition? Under current law, a recall is a genuine off-cycle opportunity for the minority party to gain an executive office (as in 2003). Under Prop 5, a successful recall yields a same-party successor (Lt Gov or gubernatorial appointee). Given Democrats hold every statewide office, this means recalls would essentially never transfer power. Is that bad? One view: recalls are supposed to be about misconduct removal, not power transfer; the regular election is where power transfers happen. Another view: weakening the recall as a tool of accountability while leaving the low signature threshold in place is a half-measure that mainly serves incumbents.

Note the important asymmetry: Prop 5 does not make recalls harder to initiate; it keeps the removal question intact. Voters still can remove an official by majority. So the "accountability" function is preserved — indeed arguably strengthened, because voters who want removal but fear an unknown/undesirable replacement will no longer be deterred from voting yes on removal.

Actually that's a notable point in favor: the current two-question system can suppress the removal vote (voters who want the official gone but fear the successor). Removing question 2 makes the recall a pure accountability vote. Opponents argue the reverse (that voters will fear being unrepresented). Both speculative.

Given: (1) the fix of a genuine democratic defect (successors with less support than the retained incumbent — documented in every successful CA recall), (2) the conflict-of-interest fix, (3) alignment with most other states and with existing vacancy rules, (4) support from nonpartisan good-government organizations spanning the ideological spectrum (LWV, Common Cause, a Republican former FPPC chair, McClatchy), (5) negligible fiscal impact, and (6) preservation of the recall power itself — I lean YES.

The NO case rests heavily on partisan grievance, a preference for immediate replacement, and one drafting wart (recalled officer may run in the special election) that is real but modest. Also the fact that most editorial boards oppose is a signal, but their reasons are split (some want more reform, some want less) and several are motivated by protecting the minority party's path to power.

Hmm, but let me weigh the "appointed successor for statewide offices" concern once more. Suppose voters recall the Attorney General (say for failing to prosecute something). Under Prop 5, the Governor appoints a new AG, subject to legislative confirmation, who serves the rest of the term. In a state with Democratic supermajorities, that means the recalled AG is replaced by another Democrat chosen by the Governor. The voters' removal achieves... removal of the individual, yes, but no policy change. Under current law, the replacement could be from another party. Is that a meaningful loss? The recall of an AG for cause should still mean removal. And the appointee still has to run in the next regular election? Hmm, under existing law, appointees to constitutional offices serve the remainder of the unexpired term (no interim election). So potentially up to ~3.5 years unelected. That's the strongest NO point.

But note the same is already true for AG vacancies by resignation/death (Becerra after Harris; Bonta after Becerra) — Californians accept gubernatorial appointment with legislative confirmation. So Prop 5 introduces no new concentration of power; it extends existing, familiar rules.

On balance: YES.

Let me do a couple more checks for completeness: Is there anything in the measure with a hidden catch (e.g., effective date, applicability to pending recalls, changing signature requirements)? The text shows only Sections 15, 17 of Article II and Section 10 of Article V. Section 15(a)-(b) unchanged (recall election timing). No signature changes. No retroactivity clause apparent. Let me check the full SCA 1 text for an effective date/operative provision. The proposed law text as printed seems complete (three sections). There may also be a Section 4 in the resolution about... but the VIG printed only those. Good.

Also let me double-check the LAO analysis statement about who calls a special election for a recalled legislator and how long the seat stays vacant — the LAO says "a replacement typically would be elected through a separate special election." Under Elections Code 10400 et seq., the Governor must call a special election for a legislative vacancy within 14 days, held ~ 63-105 days later... Let me not over-verify; the CalMatters said "within about four months."

One more consideration: the "Fix the Recall" campaign — does it have bipartisan support? Let me check quickly whether any Republicans/independents support (Dan Schnur is a Republican former FPPC chair — that's notable). Also Lt. Gov. Eleni Kounalakis supports (self-interested but fine).

I think I have enough. Let me also quickly check the Voice of San Diego debate for Chris Ward's Democratic critique, to make sure I'm not missing something important. And check whether there's any legal analysis suggesting Prop 5 could create a constitutional conflict (e.g., if the recalled officer wins the special election, can they be recalled again? six-month bar).

Let me do one more fetch of the Voice of San Diego piece.

I have enough research. Let me do a final sanity check on a couple of remaining uncertainties:

1. Does the recalled officer's ability to run in a special election apply to gubernatorial special elections? Yes — the text says "the officer who was the subject of the recall election shall not be appointed to fill the vacancy," which implies they may be a candidate. For the governor, the special election would be for governor, and the recalled governor could run. Hmm, that's a significant flaw: a governor recalled for misconduct could immediately run to win back the office. But voters who just recalled them by majority are unlikely to re-elect them months later in a higher-turnout... actually the special election is consolidated with a statewide primary/general — decent turnout. Still, the electorate that recalled them would be the same electorate.

2. Is there any provision that would apply Prop 5 retroactively to any pending recall? SOS says no current recall efforts.

Final decision. Let me think once more about which side is "better" from a neutral, public-interest standpoint.

The core empirical fact: In all six successful California state recalls, the successor won with less than a majority; in Newman's case, more voters voted "no recall" than voted for the winning successor. That's an objective democratic deficit. Prop 5 fixes it in a way that mirrors existing vacancy rules used for death/resignation, and it adds majority-runoff special elections for early-term gubernatorial recalls. It also fixes the Lt. Governor conflict of interest.

The downsides: delay in representation for legislative seats (months), possible long-term unelected appointees for statewide offices, and the odd permission for a recalled officer to run for the seat again. It doesn't address the low signature threshold.

Is the downside fatal? The "recalled officer may run again" provision is genuinely bad drafting, but it does not overturn a recall (the removal still happens; they'd have to win a majority in a subsequent election). And it can be fixed later by statute? Hmm — actually, since it's a constitutional amendment deleting a constitutional bar, the Legislature could later restore a bar via statute or another amendment. So the flaw is correctable.

The "appointments for statewide offices" concern is inherent in existing law for all other vacancies and includes legislative confirmation.

The "representation gap" concern is inherent in existing law for legislative vacancies too.

So Prop 5 essentially says: recalls should follow normal vacancy rules, and removal should be a clean majority question. On balance, that improves legitimacy and reduces the "recall as partisan lottery" incentive, at the cost of immediacy.

Counter-consideration on partisan fairness/entrenchment: it does mean that in a one-party state, recalls can't flip an office. But recall isn't designed as a power-transfer mechanism; regular elections are. And the removal threat itself remains.

Given the weight of nonpartisan good-government support (LWV, Common Cause, former FPPC chair, Sacramento Bee/McClatchy, SPUR, LA Times columnists, Secretary of State), the LAO's negligible fiscal impact, and the objective defect it corrects, I'll answer "yes."

Hmm, but let me consider one more time whether the strongest arguments point the other way. The majority of newspaper editorial boards say no; public opinion says no by wide margins. But popularity and editorial-board counts aren't the merits. Also, the "no" arguments in the official guide (from the Senate Minority Leader) are essentially partisan and rhetorical ("gaslighting," "sour grapes") — the strongest substantive NO points are: (a) loss of voter choice of successor, particularly for governor where the Lt Gov (same ticket/party) would take over for the remainder of the term; (b) unelected appointments for other statewide offices; (c) representation gaps; (d) recalled officer can run again; (e) doesn't fix the low signature threshold.

Point (a) deserves more weight: for the most powerful office, Prop 5 means voters who remove a governor could get a same-party governor for up to 2 years with no election, or the remainder of the term. Under current law they'd choose a successor immediately. That's a substantive diminishment of the recall's potency as a tool for political change. But note: the Lt Gov was elected statewide in a two-candidate majority runoff by the same electorate in the same cycle — the second-most-endorsed statewide ticket. And under Prop 5, early-term recalls trigger a majority-vote special election. So for a governor recalled in the first two years (the scenario in which a change of direction would matter most, with the most time remaining), voters do get to elect a successor by majority. The "no election at all" case only applies in the last two years — when a regular election is close anyway (max 2 years, often less). That substantially mitigates the concern. Actually the current vacancy law already gives the Lt Gov the entire remainder of the term with no election; Prop 5 improves on that.

So on the gubernatorial side, Prop 5 is roughly neutral-to-better than existing vacancy norms, and somewhat less direct than current recall law but with higher legitimacy for the successor (majority requirement).

OK. I'm fairly comfortable with YES. Let me also make sure I'm not missing a "poison pill" in the measure — e.g., does it also affect judges (Supreme Court justices can be recalled / retained)? Article II Section 15 applies to "an officer"; the amendment mentions "nor shall there be any candidacy for an office filled pursuant to subdivision (d) of Section 16 of Article VI" — that's about appellate justices' vacancies? Actually Article VI Section 16(d) deals with filling vacancies in the Supreme Court/Courts of Appeal (governor appoints with Commission on Judicial Appointments confirmation). The deleted text: "The officer may not be a candidate, nor shall there be any candidacy for an office filled pursuant to subdivision (d) of Section 16 of Article VI." So current law bars candidacy for judicial offices filled under that provision. Prop 5 deletes that clause — meaning... hmm, for judicial vacancies filled by appointment under Art VI §16(d), there would be no candidacy anyway. Minor.

Also, can judges be recalled in California? Article II Section 14: "Recall is the power of the electors to remove an elective officer." Justices of the Supreme Court can be recalled? Actually California voters can remove justices through retention elections (Art VI §16(a)) — not recall. The SOS page said recalls apply to state officers including justices? The recall procedures guide says "Any state officer may be recalled. These include the elected offices of Governor, Lieutenant Governor, ... members of the Legislature, Board of Equalization, judges of the Courts of Appeal and Supreme Court justices"? Let me not worry.

Final answer: yes.

Wait — I should double check one thing: the user gave a URL that resolves to the 2026 Prop 5 (recall reform). I researched that. Good.

The answer format: "Answer with only `yes` or `no`." I'll answer "yes" only.

Prop 5 fixes it in a way that mirrors existing vacancy rules used for death/resignation, and it adds majority-runoff special elections for early-term gubernatorial recalls. It also fixes the Lt. Governor conflict of interest.

The downsides: delay in representation for legislative seats (months), possible long-term unelected appointees for statewide offices, and the odd permission for a recalled officer to run for the seat again. It doesn't address the low signature threshold.

Is the downside fatal? The "recalled officer may run again" provision is genuinely bad drafting, but it does not overturn a recall (the removal still happens; they'd have to win a majority in a subsequent election). And it can be fixed later by statute? Hmm — actually, since it's a constitutional amendment deleting a constitutional bar, the Legislature could later restore a bar via statute or another amendment. So the flaw is correctable.

The "appointments for statewide offices" concern is inherent in existing law for all other vacancies and includes legislative confirmation.

The "representation gap" concern is inherent in existing law for legislative vacancies too.

So Prop 5 essentially says: recalls should follow normal vacancy rules, and removal should be a clean majority question. On balance, that improves legitimacy and reduces the "recall as partisan lottery" incentive, at the cost of immediacy.

Counter-consideration on partisan fairness/entrenchment: it does mean that in a one-party state, recalls can't flip an office. But recall isn't designed as a power-transfer mechanism; regular elections are. And the removal threat itself remains.

Given the weight of nonpartisan good-government support (LWV, Common Cause, former FPPC chair, Sacramento Bee/McClatchy, SPUR, LA Times columnists, Secretary of State), the LAO's negligible fiscal impact, and the objective defect it corrects, I'll answer "yes."

Hmm, but let me consider one more time whether the strongest arguments point the other way. The majority of newspaper editorial boards say no; public opinion says no by wide margins. But popularity and editorial-board counts aren't the merits. Also, the "no" arguments in the official guide (from the Senate Minority Leader) are essentially partisan and rhetorical ("gaslighting," "sour grapes") — the strongest substantive NO points are: (a) loss of voter choice of successor, particularly for governor where the Lt Gov (same ticket/party) would take over for the remainder of the term; (b) unelected appointments for other statewide offices; (c) representation gaps; (d) recalled officer can run again; (e) doesn't fix the low signature threshold.

Point (a) deserves more weight: for the most powerful office, Prop 5 means voters who remove a governor could get a same-party governor for up to 2 years with no election, or the remainder of the term. Under current law they'd choose a successor immediately. That's a substantive diminishment of the recall's potency as a tool for political change. But note: the Lt Gov was elected statewide in a two-candidate majority runoff by the same electorate in the same cycle — the second-most-endorsed statewide ticket. And under Prop 5, early-term recalls trigger a majority-vote special election. So for a governor recalled in the first two years (the scenario in which a change of direction would matter most, with the most time remaining), voters do get to elect a successor by majority. The "no election at all" case only applies in the last two years — when a regular election is close anyway (max 2 years, often less). That substantially mitigates the concern. Actually the current vacancy law already gives the Lt Gov the entire remainder of the term with no election; Prop 5 improves on that.

So on the gubernatorial side, Prop 5 is roughly neutral-to-better than existing vacancy norms, and somewhat less direct than current recall law but with higher legitimacy for the successor (majority requirement).
